## Objective

How population-level ecological release scales to community-level trait assembly across a gradient of ecologically similar sites with declining species richness? 

![Conceptual framework illustrating three hypotheses for how ecological release at the population-level may scale to community-level patterns in functional trait space.](figures jpg/Figure 1 - Conceptual_arrows.jpg)

Species-poor communities may show expansion in functional space (\textbf{Hypothesis 1: Expansion}). Reduced interspecific competition on islands allows species to exploit peripheral regions of the functional space. Functionally distinctive species may increase in abundance or expand their niche, leading to higher trait variability. We expect increases in the ranges of trait dimensions and extreme trait values, particularly in traits contributing to individual survival and fitness. Some of these traits may include dispersal morphology (e.g., wing shape), foraging morphology (e.g., tarsus length), and dietary morphology (e.g., beak shape). 

Communities may show a shift in functional space rather than expansion (\textbf{Hypothesis 2: Shift}). Reduced predation on islands may drive species to modify behavioral and ecological strategies without necessarily expanding functional trait spaces, which can remain constrained by higher intraspecific competition ([MacArthur 1972](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1934090), [Terborgh 2023](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jbi.14530)). This shift may manifest as changes in the dominant trait dimensions, such as an increased use of lower vertical strata ([MacArthur 1972](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1934090)), or an increased reproductive niche breadth, resulting in a higher number of nest structures and nest locations in species-poor communities. Still, in this scenario, variance among trait values remains similar. 

Ultimately, these two hypotheses may be applied simultaneously. Communities may show functional space expansion and shift of combined functional traits through joint release (\textbf{Hypothesis 3: Expansion + Shift}). When competition and predation pressures are relaxed, we may expect a synergistic effect of functional trait space, resulting in combined expansion and shift. This could result in increased trait diversity (higher variance), different trait dominance (mean), and reorganization of community-level trait distributions. Mechanistically, this reflects niche expansion and niche shift, driven by changes in abundance, behavior, and ecological strategies, accompanied by reduced competition and predation ([MacArthur 1972](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1934090), [Herrmann et al. 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169534720303116)). 

To compare these hypotheses, we analyzed data on birds--a diverse taxonomic group for which functional traits are well described at the species level ([Tobias et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.13898), [Sheard et al. 2023](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/geb.13783), [Moura et al. 2024](https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3002658), [Şekercioğlu et al. 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-05615-3)) . Bird communities have also been a classic case study in ecological release and density compensation in mainland-island gradients ([Lack 1944](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1474-919X.1944.tb04092.x), [MacArthur 1972](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1934090), [Lack 1976 - see Orians 1976](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.194.4270.1153), [Cox & Ricklefs 1977](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3543330?seq=1), [Wright & Steadman 2012](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2699.2012.02754.x), [Sherry et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/ukaa049)). Specifically, we compared two regions with known gradients of species richness and high levels of bird endemism that have been foundational to island biogeography: the Caribbean and Eastern Indo-Pacific meta-archipelagos.

## Packages

The packages used are

```{r packages, echo=TRUE}
# For code 1 - Islands eBird filtering
library(tidyverse); #manipulate data
library(auk); #eBird data filters
library(dggridR) #Spatiotemporal Subsampling
library(sf) # Simple Features, to encode spatial vector data
```

## Islands eBird filtering

We downloaded all eBird data up to January 2026. To reduce the size of this files and filter accordingly to our aim, we select species considered Sedentary or Resident that do NOT occupy specific primary habitats Sea, Wetland, Riparian, or Coastal (only "land birds"), using the Mobility and Habitat trait groups in [Şekercioğlu et al. (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-05615-3). We combine the eBird taxonomy with different bird trait databases to generate a list of taxa to filter in eBird (the code could be names as `0_resident_landbirds_list.R`):

```{r eBird list matching taxonomy of functional traits, eval=FALSE}
# eBird at 2025 will be my taxonomy (to filter in the ebd file)
eBird_taxonomy <- read_csv("FunctionalTraits/eBird-Clements_v2025-integrated-checklist-October-2025.csv") |> 
  select(scientific_name = `scientific name`, 
         category)

# BIRDBASE is more updated than AVONET, including Distribution, Body Mass, Elevation, Habitat, Diet, Reproductive Behavior, Demography, and Mobility
birdbase <- read_csv("FunctionalTraits/BirdBase.csv") |> 
  # only sedentary or resident species NOT from the Sea, Wetland, Riparian, or Coastal primary habitat
  filter(`Mobility - Sedentary or Resident` == 1,
         `Habitat - Primary Habitat` != "Sea", 
         `Habitat - Primary Habitat` != "Wetland", 
         `Habitat - Primary Habitat` != "Riparian",
         `Habitat - Primary Habitat` != "Coastal") |>
  # adjust traits for functional space estimation
  mutate(ESI = log10(100 / (`Habitat - Habitat Breadth` * (`Diet - Diet Breadth` + 0.1))), 
         `Body mass` = log(`Body Mass - Average`), 
         `Clutch size` = ((`Reproductive Behavior - Max Clutch Size` + `Reproductive Behavior - Min Clutch Size`) / 2),
         `Number of broods` = ((`Reproductive Behavior - Max Number of Broods` + `Reproductive Behavior - Min Number of Broods`) / 2),
         `Nest location breadth` = str_count(`Reproductive Behavior - Nest Substrate`, "[A-Za-z]"), 
         `Nest type breadth` = ifelse(`Reproductive Behavior - Nest Type` == "", 0, str_count(`Reproductive Behavior - Nest Type`, ",") + 1))

# long format of birdbase to try and harmonize taxonomies
birdbase_long <- birdbase |>
  pivot_longer(    
    cols = c(`Latin (BirdLife_IOC_Clements_AviList)`,
             `HBW/BirdLife International (v9.1)`,
             `IOC World Bird List (v15.1)`,
             `eBird/Clements (V2024b)`,
             `AviList v1 2025`),    
    names_to = "taxonomy_source_birdbase",    
    values_to = "species_name"  
    ) |>
  filter(!is.na(species_name))

# AVONET

# the raw data from Tobias et al.
avonet <- read_csv("ELEData/TraitData/AVONET_Raw_Data.csv")

# long format of avonet to try and harmonize taxonomies
avonet_long <- avonet |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Species1_BirdLife, 
             Species2_eBird, 
             Species3_BirdTree, 
             eBird.species.group),
    names_to = "taxonomy_source_avonet",
    values_to = "species_name"  
    ) |>
  group_by(taxonomy_source_avonet, species_name) |>
  summarise(
    `Hand Wing Index` = mean(`Hand-wing.Index`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Tarsus length` = mean(`Tarsus.Length`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Wing length` = mean(`Wing.Length`, na.rm = TRUE), 
    `Beak length (nares)` = mean(`Beak.Length_Nares`, na.rm = TRUE), 
    `Beak length (culmen)` = mean(`Beak.Length_Culmen`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Beak width` = mean(`Beak.Width`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Beak depth` = mean(`Beak.Depth`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# TetrapodsTraits
tetrapods <- read_csv("FunctionalTraits/TetrapodTraits_1.0.0.csv") |>
  filter(Class %in% "Aves")

# long format of tetrapods to try and harmonize taxonomies
tetra_long <- tetrapods |>
  pivot_longer(    
    cols = c(Scientific.Name, 
             IUCN_Binomial),    
    names_to = "taxonomy_source_tetrapods",    
    values_to = "species_name"  
    )

# Join and summarize per "taxa" (it will include subspecies and groups in eBird)

ebird_functional_taxa <- eBird_taxonomy |>
  left_join(birdbase_long, by = c("scientific_name" = "species_name")) |>
  left_join(avonet_long, by = c("scientific_name" = "species_name")) |> 
  left_join(tetra_long, by = c("scientific_name" = "species_name")) |>
  filter(!is.na(scientific_name)) |>
  group_by(scientific_name) |>
  summarise(`log (Body mass)` = mean(`Body mass`, na.rm = TRUE), # this already have the log transformation from birdbase
            `Hand Wing Index` = mean(`Hand Wing Index`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Tarsus length` = mean(`Tarsus length`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Wing length` = mean(`Wing length`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Beak length (nares)` = mean(`Beak length (nares)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Beak length (culmen)` = mean(`Beak length (culmen)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Beak width` = mean(`Beak width`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Beak depth` = mean(`Beak depth`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Diet breadth` = mean(`Diet - Diet Breadth`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Habitat breadth` = mean(`Habitat - Habitat Breadth`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `EcoloSpeciIndex` = mean(ESI, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Verticality index` = mean(`Verticality`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Elevational range` = mean(`Elevation - Elevational Range`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Clutch size` = mean(`Clutch size`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Number of broods` = mean(`Number of broods`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Nest location breadth` = mean(`Nest location breadth`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Nest type breadth` = mean(`Nest type breadth`, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  unique()
saveRDS(ebird_functional_taxa, "FunctionalTraits/eBird_func_taxa.RDS")
```

Note that we saved the `.RDS` file, which is an object in `R` to facilitate transferring across systems/computers and backup without running again the code.

Now we can apply the filter for resident landbird "species" in the two meta archipelagos. To use the ebd files (big files), we should decompress them from a `.tar` archive and a `.txt.gz` compressed file. We can use the Terminal for this, with the command `tar -0xf ebd_relJan-2026.tar ebd_relJan-2026.txt.gz | gunzip > ebd_relJan-2026.txt`, which uses a pipe (`|`) and a redirection (`>`) to the folder that will contain the `.txt` file (same as the `.tar`: `ebd_txt_files`). With that file extracted, we can run the next code in the Terminal. But even better, the use of [HiPerGator](https://docs.rc.ufl.edu/) at UF would facilitate this process, although it requires a "scheduler" (`sbatch`) file to run specific codes.

First, we download the ebd file from [eBird](https://ebird.org/data/download/ebd). The file is 220 GB in `.tar` (decompressed is almost 900 GB!). So, we use [Globus](https://docs.rc.ufl.edu/data_transfer/globus/) to transfer the downloaded `.tar` file to the HiPerGator. Once there, we create the `sbatch` for decompressing the `.tar` (`.txt.gz`) to `.txt`. We named this scheduler as `extract_ebd.sh`, located in the same folder `funbiog_eBird/ebd_txt_files` to be run.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH --job-name=extract_ebd     # Job name 
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL          # Mail events 
#SBATCH --mail-user=oacevedocharry@ufl.edu     # Where to send mail 
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                    # Run on a single CPU 
#SBATCH --mem=4gb                     # Job memory request 
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00               # Time limit hrs:min:sec 
#SBATCH --output=extract_ebd_%j.log   # Standard output and error log 
pwd; hostname; date 

echo "Running decompress of ebd file on a single CPU core" 

tar -xOf ebd_relJan-2026.tar ebd_relJan-2026.txt.gz | gunzip > ebd_relJan-2026.txt

date
```

Once the file is created, we run through the Terminal (logged in the HiPerGator) as `sbatch extract_ebd.sh`. We can check the process with `squeue -u oacevedocharry`, with the status (`ST`) running indicated by `R`

```{r eval=FALSE}
[oacevedocharry@login7 ebd_txt_files]$ sbatch extract_ebd.sh 
Submitted batch job 37330555
[oacevedocharry@login7 ebd_txt_files]$ squeue -u oacevedocharry
             JOBID PARTITION     NAME     USER ST       TIME  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
          37330555 hpg-milan extract_ oacevedo  R       1:46      1 c0709a-s2
```

This process of creating a scheduler to run complex codes will be used for all HiPerGator processes. For instance, for the filtering of the data from the `funbiog_eBird` folder. We generate the `R` code (`1_a_filtering_eBird.R`):

```{r 1_a_filtering_eBird, eval=FALSE}
########################################
###~ eBird data - Island filtering 2026 ~####
########################################

#Packages
library(auk); #eBird data filters
library(tidyverse); #manipulate data
library(dggridR) #Spatiotemporal Subsampling
library(sf) # Simple Features, to encode spatial vector data

taxa_etal <- readRDS("FunctionalTraits/eBird_func_taxa.RDS") |>
  dplyr::select(scientific_name) |> 
  as.vector()

#Define the geographic range
CaribbeanRange <- c(-91,8,-59,27)
IndoMalayRange <- c(90,-20,180,20)

#select the columns to extract (based on x$col_idx$name)
colsE <- c("observer_id", "sampling_event_identifier",
           "group identifier",
           "common_name", "scientific_name",
           "observation_count",
           "country", "state_code", "locality_id", "latitude", "longitude",
           "observation_type", "all_species_reported",
           "observation_date",
           "time_observations_started",
           "duration_minutes", "effort_distance_km",
           "number_observers")

f_ebd_Ca <- "ebd_txt_files/ebd_Caribbean.txt" #Temporal file to save the filtering eBird data (records)

f_ebd_IM <- "ebd_txt_files/ebd_IndoMalayan.txt" #Temporal file to save the filtering eBird data (records)

ebd_filtCarib<-auk_ebd("ebd_txt_files/ebd_relJan-2026.txt") %>%
  auk_bbox(CaribbeanRange) %>% #W, S, E, N
  auk_year(c(2015:2025)) %>%
  auk_protocol(c("Traveling", "Stationary")) %>%
  auk_distance(distance = c(0,5)) %>%
  auk_duration(duration = c(0,300))%>%
  auk_complete() %>%
  auk_filter(f_ebd_Ca, overwrite=T, keep = colsE)

ebd_filtIndoM<-auk_ebd("ebd_txt_files/ebd_relJan-2026.txt") %>%
  auk_bbox(IndoMalayRange) %>% #W, S, E, N
  auk_year(c(2015:2025)) %>%
  auk_protocol(c("Traveling", "Stationary")) %>%
  auk_distance(distance = c(0,5)) %>%
  auk_duration(duration = c(0,300))%>%
  auk_complete() %>%
  auk_filter(f_ebd_IM, overwrite=T, keep = colsE)

# and with read_ebd I apply another filter to do not repeat records from groups
ebd_Caribbean <- read_ebd(f_ebd_Ca) |>
  mutate(Meta.Archipelago = "Caribbean")
ebd_IndoMalayan <- read_ebd(f_ebd_IM) |>
  mutate(Meta.Archipelago = "IndoMalayan")

# Function to convert time observation to hours since midnight
time_to_decimal <- function(x) {
  x <- hms(x, quiet = TRUE)
  hour(x) + minute(x) / 60 + second(x) / 3600
}

#Effort data
#Caribbean data
Carib_eff <- ebd_Caribbean |>
  mutate(
    # I don't want count in X, to convert to NA
    observation_count = as.integer(observation_count),
    # effort_distance_km to 0 for non-travelling counts
    effort_distance_km = if_else(observation_type == "Stationary",
                                 0, effort_distance_km),
    # convert time to decimal hours since midnight
    time_observations_started = time_to_decimal(time_observations_started),
    hour_sampling = round(time_observations_started, 0),
    # split date into year, month, week, and day of year
    year = year(observation_date),
    month = month(observation_date),
    week = week(observation_date),
    day_of_year = yday(observation_date),
    # temporal aggregation - month
    Time.t = case_when(year == 2015 ~ month,
                       year > 2015 ~ month+(12*(year-2015)))) |>
  filter(number_observers <= 10,         #Only list with less than 10 observers
         effort_distance_km <= 5,        #be sure of distance effort
         duration_minutes %in% (0:300), #be sure of duration effort
         !is.na(observation_count))      #only records with abundance estimation

Checklists_with_more_SppC <- Carib_eff %>%
  dplyr::select(checklist_id, scientific_name) %>%
  group_by(checklist_id) %>%
  summarise(N_species = n()) %>%
  filter(N_species >= quantile(N_species, 0.25)) # minimum number of species per sampling - 1st Quartile

Caribbean_cooc <- Carib_eff[Carib_eff$checklist_id %in% Checklists_with_more_SppC$checklist_id, ]

saveRDS(Caribbean_cooc, "results_funbiog/Caribbean_cooc.RDS")

#And now with the Oriental-Indo_Malayan-Papuan-Melanesian
IndoM_eff <- ebd_IndoMalayan |>
  mutate(
    # I don't want here count in X, to convert to NA
    observation_count = as.integer(observation_count),
    # effort_distance_km to 0 for non-travelling counts
    effort_distance_km = if_else(observation_type == "Stationary",
                                 0, effort_distance_km),
    # convert time to decimal hours since midnight
    time_observations_started = time_to_decimal(time_observations_started),
    hour_sampling = round(time_observations_started, 0),
    # split date into year, month, week, and day of year
    year = year(observation_date),
    month = month(observation_date),
    week = week(observation_date),
    day_of_year = yday(observation_date),
    # temporal aggregation - month
    Time.t = case_when(year == 2015 ~ month,
                       year > 2015 ~ month+(12*(year-2015)))) |>
  filter(number_observers <= 10,         #Only list with less than 10 observers
         effort_distance_km <= 5,        #be sure of distance effort
         duration_minutes %in% (0:300), #be sure of duration effort
         !is.na(observation_count))      #remove records without abundance estimation

Checklists_with_more_SppIP <- IndoM_eff %>%
  dplyr::select(checklist_id, scientific_name) %>%
  group_by(checklist_id) %>%
  summarise(N_species = n()) %>%
  filter(N_species >= quantile(N_species, 0.25)) # minimum number of species per sampling - 1st Quartile

IndoMalayan_cooc <- IndoM_eff[IndoM_eff$checklist_id %in% Checklists_with_more_SppIP$checklist_id, ]

saveRDS(IndoMalayan_cooc, "results_funbiog/IndoMalayan_cooc.RDS")

##Spatial Grids ####

# Spatiotemporal Subsampling in diameters of ~11 km (area of ~100 km^2)
# spacing 1 correspond to Characteristic Length Scale, or diameter of spherical cell
dggs_island <- dgconstruct(spacing = 11) 

#add a new variable that identify cell
Caribbean_cooc_cells <- Caribbean_cooc |>
  mutate(cell = dgGEO_to_SEQNUM(dggs_island, #id for cells
                                longitude, latitude)$seqnum) |>
  group_by(cell, scientific_name, Time.t) |>
  # extract the minimum number of individual detected per month per cell of each species
  mutate(Observed.y = round(max(observation_count))) |> 
  ungroup()

# filter cells with more than 25% (1stQ) localities within
cells_1stQ_Ca <- Caribbean_cooc_cells |>
  group_by(cell, locality_id) |>
  count() |>
  group_by(cell) |>
  count() |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(n >= quantile(n, 0.25))

Caribbean_SS = Caribbean_cooc_cells[Caribbean_cooc_cells$cell %in% cells_1stQ_Ca$cell, ]

saveRDS(Caribbean_SS, "results_funbiog/Caribbean_SS.RDS")

# we can extract the list of species per cell as:

Caribbean_List_Spp <- Caribbean_SS |>
  group_by(cell, scientific_name) |>
  summarise(count=n())

saveRDS(Caribbean_List_Spp, "results_funbiog/Caribbean_List_Spp.RDS")

# Get the number of records in each cell
RichnessCell_Ca   <- Caribbean_SS %>%
  group_by(cell, scientific_name) %>%
  summarise(count=n()) %>%
  group_by(cell) %>%
  summarise(SpRichness=n())

# Get the grid cell boundaries for cells which had quakes
gridCaribbean <- dgcellstogrid(dggs_island, RichnessCell_Ca$cell)

# Update the grid cells' properties to include the number of lists in each cell
gridCaribbean <- merge(gridCaribbean, RichnessCell_Ca, by.x = "seqnum", by.y = "cell")

# Handle cells that cross 180 degrees
wrapped_grid_Caribbean = st_wrap_dateline(gridCaribbean,
                                         options = c("WRAPDATELINE=YES","DATELINEOFFSET=180"), quiet = TRUE)

saveRDS(wrapped_grid_Caribbean, "results_funbiog/wrapped_grid_Caribbean.rds")

# and the IndoMalayan
#add a new variable that identify cell
IndoMalayan_cooc_cells <- IndoMalayan_cooc |>
  mutate(cell = dgGEO_to_SEQNUM(dggs_island, #id for cells
                                longitude, latitude)$seqnum) |>
  group_by(cell, scientific_name, Time.t) |>
  # extract the minimum number of individual detected per month per cell of each species
  mutate(Observed.y = round(max(observation_count))) |> 
  ungroup()

# filter cells with more than 25% (1stQ) localities within
cells_1stQ_IM <- IndoMalayan_cooc_cells |>
  group_by(cell, locality_id) |>
  count() |>
  group_by(cell) |>
  count() |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(n >= quantile(n, 0.25))

IndoMalayan_SS = IndoMalayan_cooc_cells[IndoMalayan_cooc_cells$cell %in% cells_1stQ_Ca$cell, ]

saveRDS(IndoMalayan_SS, "results_funbiog/IndoMalayan_SS.RDS")

# we can extract the list of species per cell as:

IndoMalayan_List_Spp <- IndoMalayan_SS |>
  group_by(cell, scientific_name) |>
  summarise(count=n())

saveRDS(IndoMalayan_List_Spp, "results_funbiog/IndoMalayan_List_Spp.RDS")

# Get the number of records in each cell
RichnessCell_IM   <- IndoMalayan_SS %>%
  group_by(cell, scientific_name) %>%
  summarise(count=n()) %>%
  group_by(cell) %>%
  summarise(SpRichness=n())

# Get the grid cell boundaries for cells which had quakes
gridIndoMalayan <- dgcellstogrid(dggs_island, RichnessCell_IM$cell)

# Update the grid cells' properties to include the number of lists in each cell
gridIndoMalayan <- merge(gridIndoMalayan, RichnessCell_IM, by.x = "seqnum", by.y = "cell")

# Handle cells that cross 180 degrees
wrapped_grid_IndoMalayan = st_wrap_dateline(gridIndoMalayan,
                                         options = c("WRAPDATELINE=YES","DATELINEOFFSET=180"), quiet = TRUE)

saveRDS(wrapped_grid_IndoMalayan, "results_funbiog/wrapped_grid_IndoMalayan.rds")

#End of this code
```

And then, make the scheduler (`island_filtering.sh`) to run this code:

```{r eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=Islands_filtering_eBird  # Job name
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL                    # Mail events
#SBATCH --mail-user=oacevedocharry@ufl.edu # Where to send mail
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                         # Number of processes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16                 # Number of CPU cores per task or process
#SBATCH --mem=128gb                         # Increase per processor memory
#SBATCH --time=30-00:00:00                    # Time limit hrs:min:sec
#SBATCH --output=Islands_filtering_eBird_%j.log             # Standard output and error log
#SBATCH --qos=rcstudents
pwd; hostname; date

echo Working directory is $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

#loading modules for R
module purge
module load R

#Run R script
Rscript 1_a_filtering_eBird.R

date
```

Recall, the scheduler is run through the Terminal connected to the HiPerGator with the command `sbatch island_filtering.sh`.



## Organizing eBird data for stationary distribution population models

At the core of our question is the estimation of a expected log-abundance at stationary distribution to weight the functional traits. We used the Stochastic Gompertz State-Space model (see [Dennis & Ponciano](https://doi.org/10.1890/13-1486.1)). 

The stochastic differential equation describing the dynamic is:
$$
dN(t) = \theta N(t)[\log \kappa - \log N(t)] dt + \beta N(t) dW(t)
$$
\noindent in which over a tiny time interval, $dt$, an increment of abundance $dN(t)$ is drawn from a normal distribution with a mean $\theta N(t)[\log \kappa - \log N(t)] dt$ and variance $[\beta N(t)]^2 dt$, where $N(t)$ denotes the current abundance, $t$ the current time of population trajectory, $\theta$ and $\kappa$ are constants of equilibrium abundance and speed of equilibrium, respectively. This dynamic is updated as $N(t) + dN(t)$ and $t + dt$. An infinitesimal increment of the Gompertz growth deterministic skeleton (in ordinary differential form $\frac{dn(t)}{dt} = \theta n(t)[\log \kappa - \log n(t)]$) is perturbed by a random noise $dW(t) \sim \text{Normal}(0, dt)$, in which intensity of the noise is scaled by $\beta N(t)$ with $\beta > 0$, denoting the environmental stochasticity. This is a diffusion process with infinitesimal mean $m(n) = \theta n(\log \kappa - \log n)$ and infinitesimal variance $v(n) = \beta^2n^2$. Let $X(t) = g(N(t))$ be a smooth invertible transformation (e.g., $\log N(t)$), the infinitesimal mean $m_{X}$ and variance $v_X$ of $X(t)$ are given by the Itô transformation formulas: $m_X(x) = m(n)g'(n) + (1/2)v(n)g''(n)$, $v_X(x) = v(n)[g'(n)]^2$, with $n = g^{-1}(x)$ and $g'$ and $g''$ representing first and second derivatives. Thus, a given diffusion process might be transformed to a scale, which exist for the stochastic Gompertz model.
